text: A huge share of real incidents start with a compromised identity, not a compromised machine — a phished password, a stolen session token, reused credentials pulled from an unrelated breach somewhere else entirely. Containing an account and containing a host are genuinely different actions aimed at genuinely different problems, and a real incident very often needs both done at the same time, not one after the other.

Account containment means disabling the account, forcing a password reset, and revoking any active sessions or tokens — a stolen session can keep working even after the password changes, which is why revocation is its own separate step. Host containment is the EDR isolation already covered: cutting the machine's network access while leaving it running for investigation.

Here's why neither one alone is enough. If an attacker has a compromised account AND a compromised host, disabling only the account leaves a foothold on the infected machine that can harvest a different credential next. Isolating only the host leaves the stolen login working from anywhere else entirely — especially for a cloud account that was never tied to that one machine in the first place.

The alert usually tells you which problem you're facing. An unfamiliar sign-in location or an MFA prompt nobody requested points to an account problem. A command-and-control beacon or EDR flagging malware on one machine points to a host problem. When both signals show up tied together — a suspicious login followed by suspicious activity from that same device — that's the signal both containment actions are needed right now.

A phishing link drops malware on a laptop, and from that laptop the attacker harvests the user's Office 365 credentials and logs into the cloud mailbox directly. The SOC disables the account and revokes its sessions, and isolates the laptop via EDR, at the same time — because doing only one leaves the other half of the attacker's access completely intact. Next up: preserving evidence while you contain.
